problem: Most zero-shot ObjectNav systems still use map-based planning for locomotion. That requires accurate depth and localization, and it is hard to plug knowledge from RGB-trained foundation models (detectors, VLMs, LLMs) into map space. End-to-end mapless open-vocabulary policies such as ZSON perform poorly because they must learn the multimodal goal alignment without large ObjectNav datasets.
motivation: Foundation models can already point at any object with a pixel. A policy that navigates toward a pixel is therefore a universal, RGB-only low-level skill for any object category and needs no text-goal alignment. Pixel-goal demonstrations are also cheap to generate at scale: every pixel of an image is a potential goal, no semantic annotation is needed, and a shortest-path planner gives optimal actions via the underlying 3D point.
key_idea: Replace the map plus path planner with a learned RGB-only pixel-goal navigation policy (PixNav). Put a GPT-4 planner on top that reasons over VLM captions of a panorama with a step-by-step Summarize, Cluster, Plan prompt, and then point to the next subgoal as a pixel via GroundingDINO and SAM.
insight:
Using pixels as the interface decouples semantic reasoning, done by frozen foundation models, from locomotion, done by a policy trained on cheap, annotation-free pixel-goal data. This gives an open-vocabulary, depth-free ObjectNav stack with 37.9 SR / 20.5 SPL on HM3D, close to the depth-and-map-based ESC (39.2/22.3).

The ablations show that explicit reminders of the goal matter mainly for longer ranges. At 1-3m all components change SR by at most 6 points (0.88 to 0.82-0.86). At 3-5m, removing the tracking head drops SR from 0.42 to 0.33 and removing goal fusion drops it to 0.34, while removing the temporal-distance head only drops it to 0.38.

PixNav transfers zero-shot to camera heights of 0.48m and 1.28m (1-3m SR 0.79/0.78) and to 100° HFOV (0.80). A narrower 60° HFOV hurts badly: 3-5m SR falls to 0.14. The LLM's spatial reasoning is only partial: it agrees with humans 68.4% on room localization and 47.1% on room clustering.
method: Pixel-goal encoding: the goal pixel (x,y) becomes a binary mask of a (2δ)-sized box (δ=2), concatenated channel-wise with the initial RGB frame. A randomly initialized 4-channel ResNet18 encodes this into a 768-d goal token, and a goal-fusion layer projects it to 256-d and concatenates it to every observation token.

PixNav policy network: a separate randomly initialized 3-channel ResNet18 embeds every history RGB frame (160x120) into 512-d tokens. A 4-layer transformer decoder integrates the full history, and three 1-layer MLP heads predict the action, the goal pixel's current location (tracking) and the remaining steps to the goal (temporal distance). The network has 54.5M parameters in total.

Training: purely supervised, loss L = L_il (action imitation) + L_track (MSE on the tracked pixel) + L_distance (MSE on remaining steps, scaled by 1/10). Discrete actions are {Stop, MoveAhead, TurnLeft, TurnRight, LookUp, LookDown}.

Data generation: in Habitat-Lab on the 80 HM3D train scenes (camera height 0.88m, HFOV 79°), a random pixel is sampled from the first RGB frame and lifted to 3D with depth. The built-in shortest-path planner then produces actions, giving more than 100,000 trajectories of at most 64 steps.

Perception: the robot rotates to capture 6 images. LLaMA-Adapter is prompted with 'Describe the room type in the image' and 'Describe the objects with details in the image' to turn each image into text. GroundingDINO + SAM segment the object chosen by the LLM, and the mask center becomes the pixel goal; the center of the selected room's 'floor' works well.

LLM planner (GPT-4) with a step-by-step prompt: (1) Summarize the captions into JSON {ID, Angle, Type, Objects}. (2) Cluster: estimate the robot's current room and position, build inter-room connections, and merge same-type rooms that are connected or at adjacent angles into a local layout graph. (3) Plan the next target, trading off exploration and exploitation. Replanning happens periodically or when PixNav finishes its subgoal.

setting.backbone: PixNav: 2x ResNet18 + 4-layer transformer decoder (trained from scratch). High level: GPT-4 (frozen) planner, LLaMA-Adapter (frozen) captioner, GroundingDINO + SAM (frozen) grounding.
setting.training_data: More than 100,000 auto-generated pixel-goal trajectories (at most 64 steps, 160x120 RGB) from 80 HM3D train scenes in Habitat, with shortest-path planner labels. No ObjectNav/semantic annotations; the LLM and VLMs are used zero-shot.
setting.observation: egocentric monocular RGB only (panorama built from 6 rotations for planning); no depth, no GPS/compass/localization at test time
setting.action_space: discrete {Stop, MoveAhead, TurnLeft, TurnRight, LookUp, LookDown} in sim; real robot {Stop, MoveAhead 0.25m, TurnLeft 30°, TurnRight 30°}
setting.privileged: none (depth and GT paths used only for training-data generation)

Real-world results appear only on the project website; no numbers are given.
results: On HM3D ObjectNav the mapless, RGB-only pipeline reaches 37.9 SR / 20.5 SPL. It clearly beats the mapless zero-shot ZSON (25.5/12.6) and approaches the depth-and-map-based ESC (39.2/22.3), which it does not surpass. Its SPL is also above the closed-set Habitat-Web (16.0). The PixNav skill alone reaches 88% SR at 1-3m but only 42% at 3-5m. It generalizes zero-shot to different camera heights and a wider HFOV, but degrades at 60° HFOV.
limitations: Long-range pixel navigation is weak (42% SR at 3-5m), and the authors themselves say long-term path planning is not satisfactory. PixNav is also sensitive to a narrower FOV (3-5m SR drops to 0.14 at 60°).

ObjectNav performance still trails the map-based ESC. The LLM's spatial reasoning is unreliable (47.1% human agreement on room clustering), and the pipeline is heavy: 6-view rotation, a VLM captioner, GPT-4, GroundingDINO and SAM for each replan.
Real-world validation is qualitative only (results on a website). The ObjectNav evaluation lacks detail on episode count and has no ablation of the LLM prompt stages.
